subject: Agriculture
title: Insects as Feed
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Insects as Feed.

hook.text: Black soldier fly larvae can convert food waste into high-protein animal feed in 14 days.

buildup.text: Traditional animal feed—soy, fishmeal—is expensive and environmentally costly. Insects could replace them.

discovery.text: Insect larvae contain 40–60% protein and thrive on organic waste that would otherwise rot in landfills.

twist.text: The EU approved insect protein for poultry and pig feed in 2021. Adoption is accelerating.

climax.text: Insect feed could break the link between livestock and deforestation by replacing soy in feed rations.

punchline.text: Feed the waste to the bugs. Feed the bugs to the chickens.

quiz.question: What is the protein content of black soldier fly larvae?

details.summary: Insect farming produces protein-rich feed for livestock and aquaculture using black soldier fly larvae, mealworms, and other species. This topic covers the environmental advantages, current commercial operations, and regulatory hurdles facing the insect-as-feed industry.
details.whyItMatters: Insects can convert organic waste into high-quality protein using a fraction of the land, water, and emissions of soybean or fishmeal production, potentially transforming the animal feed industry.
takeaways: Black soldier fly larvae can convert food waste into protein with 70% less land than soy
Insect meal contains 50–70% protein and is suitable for poultry, fish, and pig feed
The EU approved insect protein for poultry and pig feed in 2021

faq.question: How are insects used as animal feed?
faq.answer: Insects—primarily black soldier fly larvae and mealworms—are farmed on organic waste streams, harvested, dried, and processed into protein meal or oil. This insect meal replaces soybean meal or fishmeal in poultry, fish, and pig diets.

faq.question: What are the environmental benefits of insect feed?
faq.answer: Insects convert organic waste into protein using 70% less land and 50% less water than soy production. They emit far fewer greenhouse gases, can be farmed vertically in urban areas, and reduce dependence on wild-caught fishmeal for aquaculture.
